\section[vēr, aestās, autumnus, hiems]{vēr, aestās, autumnus, hiems — Latin's own four seasons}

\label{lesson:LA-C09-anni-tempora}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Four Latin nouns, one for each season — and a genuine surprise about which ones actually survived into Spanish and French as ordinary words.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The four seasons, plain and simple}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Latin} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\textbf{vēr, vēris} & \textbf{spring} \\
\textbf{aestās, aestātis} & \textbf{summer} (also just "heat") \\
\textbf{autumnus, autumnī} & \textbf{autumn} \\
\textbf{hiems, hiemis} & \textbf{winter} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{autumnus} survived plainly: it's the direct ancestor of Spanish \emph{otoño}, French \emph{automne}, and English \emph{autumn} itself — no detours.

But \textbf{vēr} and \textbf{hiems}, the plain nouns for spring and winter, mostly \textbf{didn't} make it into everyday Romance vocabulary. Instead, Spanish and French built brand-new words out of \textbf{adjective phrases} describing those seasons:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Not \emph{vēr} alone, but a Vulgar Latin phrase/reanalysis, \textbf{prīma vēra} (roughly "\textbf{first spring}") $\to$ Spanish \emph{primavera}, French (originally) \emph{primevère} — later displaced there by \emph{printemps} ("first-time," from \emph{prīmum tempus}, the very same "adjective + tempus" recipe as winter's word below; \emph{primevère} narrowed to just mean "\textbf{primrose}" today) — and Italian \emph{primavera}, still the everyday word there.
  \item Not \emph{hiems} alone, but \textbf{hībernum (tempus)}, "\textbf{the wintry {[}time{]}}" $\to$ Spanish \emph{invierno}, French \emph{hiver} — the same root as English \textbf{hibernate}.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Aestās} ("summer/heat") did survive directly into French \emph{été} — but Spanish took yet another path: it built \textbf{vērānum (tempus)} ("of spring") from \emph{vēr} itself, and that word's \emph{meaning} later drifted forward to name \textbf{summer} instead of spring, giving Spanish \emph{verano} — leaving \emph{primavera} to do spring's job.

So the picture is mixed, not a clean split: \textbf{autumnus} cruised straight through into Spanish, French, \emph{and} English unchanged; \textbf{aestās} cruised through into French (\emph{été}) but got replaced in Spanish; \textbf{vēr} and \textbf{hiems}, the plain nouns for spring and winter, essentially left \textbf{no} everyday trace in either language — both were replaced by phrase-built words instead (or, in \emph{verano}'s case, by a related word whose meaning simply moved).
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "vēr, aestās, autumnus, hiems" — the four seasons{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the one that survived plainly — "autumnus $\to$ otoño, automne, autumn"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the two built from phrases — "prīma vēra $\to$ primavera," "hībernum $\to$ invierno, hiver"{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What are Latin's four season-nouns? (\textbf{Vēr, aestās, autumnus, hiems}.) Which one survived plainly into Spanish, French, and English? (\textbf{Autumnus} $\to$ \emph{otoño, automne, autumn}.) What did Spanish and French build instead of the plain words \emph{vēr} and \emph{hiems}? (\textbf{Adjective phrases} — \emph{prīma vēra} "first spring" $\to$ \emph{primavera/primevère}; \emph{hībernum} "wintry" $\to$ \emph{invierno/hiver}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
